newsitem.title: INDONESIA: OPINION - Astra International still great value.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Astra International still great value.

text.p: PT Asia Equity Jasereh, Jakarta
JAKARTA, April 3 - Foreign shares in Indonesian automaker PT Astra International have quadrupled from a low of just Rp1,925 last June to more than Rp8,000 last month.

With the news that a major placement of 32.3 million shares has just taken place, at a discounted price of Rp7,350, some minority shareholders may wonder if those in the know are getting out while the going is good.
In our view, despite the superb performance to date and despite the placement, Astra shares still represent great value.
We believe that, to date, most of the run-up in Astra's share price has been driven by three factors:
1. The acquisitions of stakes in Astra by several major Indonesian groups;
2. A pick up in total Indonesian auto sales, with the Timor national car taking a smaller-than-expected share; and
3. Continued strong growth of motorcycle shares.
LOOKING FORWARD
Looking forward, there is a lot of other good news which does not yet appear to be fully in the price.
First, consider the Japanese yen.
Ever since late 1995, the yen has been weakening against the greenback, and its current level of Y125 per U.S. dollar is not far off a four-year low.

Given that Astra imports more than 50 percent of its automotive raw materials from its Japanese principals (including Toyoto, Isuzu and Daihatsu), there is good potential for the company to earn fatter margins in a weak yen environment.
Although most of Astra's imports are normally priced in U.S. dollars, there are quarterly revisions of the import prices to take into account exchange rate shifts.

These revisions are usually announced well after the fact, when Astra management revises its own forecast. The last management forecast for 1997 assumed an average exchange rate of 110 yen per U.S. dollar, but it now appears that the 120 yen level would be a better bet for the full year.
SUBSTITUTING EXCHANGE RATES

Simply by substituting different exchange rates into our own Asia Equity model for Astra, we estimate that every additional five yen per dollar could add more than Rp50 billion to the company's bottom line, or about 10 percent to its earnings per share.

However, if we are more conservative and assume that because of competition one-third of the benefit of a weaker yen is passed on to consumers, every additional five yen per dollar would add just over RP30 billion to the bottom line or about six percent to EPS.
In other good news, Astra's new Kijang model has gotten off to a great start, with book orders currently running at more than 27,000 units, enough to fill the next four months of production.
We expect 1997 full-year sales for the Kijang to add up to more than 75,000 units, versus just 57,000 last year.

While the passenger car side is a bit less exciting, with Astra's share down to just 24 percent in February, we note with much interest that competitor Timor Putra Nasional now plans to source components from Astra, which has 22 subsidiaries producing a range of products such as engines, shock absorbers and radiators.
MOTORCYCLES
In motorcycles, Astra's Hondas continue to dominate the industry, with the company claiming a market share of 50.4 percent in February, the most recent month for which figures are available.
In 1996 total Indonesian motorcycle sales grew by 51 percent in unit terms, and we are conservatively expecting at least another 25 percent increase this year and next.

In heavy equipment, Astra's 49.6 percent-owned PT United Tractors is set to benefit from ongoing growth in heavy equipment sales, which we project will rise by 15 percent in unit terms this year, with its market share stable at 41 percent.

Additionally, we expect United Tractors' mining division to be a big earnings driver for the company, with coal production slated to rise from two million tonnes in 1997 to eight million tonnes in 2000.
Astra's financial services division, which includes Astra Credit Company and Bank Universal, continues to experience strong growth, in part off the back of lending for cars and motorcycles.
Asia Equity estimates that Astra's contribution from financial services grew by 78 percent in 1996 and will increase by a further 68 percent this year.
PROMISING SIGNAL

Finally, there is the promising signal that in the long term Astra may expand regionally, as the company has just signed an agreement to distribute BMW sedans in Myanmar, China and Cambodia. Astra will import completely built-up units directly from Germany and initially target annual sales of 200 units in each country.
We expect Astra to report 1996 net income of approximately Rp470 billion, including RP34 billion of extraordinaries, or Rp436 billion net of them.
For 1997, we are looking at net income of Rp595 billion, which means the stock at Wednesday's closing price of Rp7,500 is trading at a very reasonable PER of 12.6x earnings.
(NOTE-The views expressed in this article represent the views of the authors only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters).
